questions.knowledge_point: Finding an Expression for a Least-Squares Regression Curve
questions.problem:
| $x$ | **$2$** | **$3$** | **$4$** | **$5$** | **$6$** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $y$ | $3$ | $-5$ | $5$ | $-4$ | $0$ |

Consider the data above and the matrices below. Find an expression for the vector of coefficients of the curve $y={\beta }_{0}+{\beta }_{1}x+{\beta }_{2}{x}^{2}$ that best fits the data. 

$$
X=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & {2}^{2} \\ 1 & 3 & {3}^{2} \\ 1 & 4 & {4}^{2} \\ 1 & 5 & {5}^{2} \\ 1 & 6 & {6}^{2}\end{aligned}],\,\beta =[\begin{aligned}{\beta }_{0} \\ {\beta }_{1} \\ {\beta }_{2}\end{aligned}],\,y=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -5 \\ 5 \\ -4 \\ 0\end{aligned}]
$$
questions.worked_solution:
The coefficients of the curve 

$$
y={\beta }_{0}+{\beta }_{1}x+{\beta }_{2}{x}^{2}
$$

that best fits the data can be found as the least-squares solution $\overset{^}{\beta }$ to the system 

$$
X\beta =y,
$$

where $X$ is the design matrix, $\beta $ is the parameter vector, and $y$ is the observation vector.

Pre-multiplying this equation by ${X}^{T},$ we obtain the corresponding normal equation

$$
{X}^{T}\,X\overset{^}{\beta }={X}^{T}y.
$$

Since the columns of $X$ are linearly independent, the matrix ${X}^{T}X$ is invertible and 

$$
\overset{^}{\beta }=({X}^{T}\,X)^{-1}{X}^{T}y.
$$

The vector of coefficients of the curve $y={\beta }_{0}+{\beta }_{1}x+{\beta }_{2}{x}^{2}$ that best fits the data above can be found using polynomial regression as 

$$
[\begin{aligned}{\beta }_{0} \\ {\beta }_{1} \\ {\beta }_{2}\end{aligned}]=({X}^{T}\,X)^{-1}{X}^{T}y,
$$

where $X$ is the corresponding design matrix and $y$ is the observation vector. Which of the following is the observation vector $y$ in this context?

| $y$ | $-20$ | $-10$ | $40$ | $20$ | $10$ |

The coefficients of the curve 

$$
y={\beta }_{0}+{\beta }_{1}x+{\beta }_{2}{x}^{2}
$$

that best fits the data can be found as the least-squares solution $\overset{^}{\beta }$ to the system 

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{X}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & {1}^{2} \\ 1 & 2 & {2}^{2} \\ 1 & 3 & {3}^{2} \\ 1 & 4 & {4}^{2} \\ 1 & 5 & {5}^{2}\end{aligned}]}}\overset{\beta }{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}{\beta }_{0} \\ {\beta }_{1} \\ {\beta }_{2}\end{aligned}]}} & =\overset{y}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}-20 \\ -10 \\ 40 \\ 20 \\ 10\end{aligned}]}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $X$ is the design matrix, $\beta $ is the parameter vector, and $y$ is the observation vector.

\begin{aligned}\overset{X}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & {1}^{2} & {1}^{3} \\ 3 & {3}^{2} & {3}^{3} \\ 5 & {5}^{2} & {5}^{3} \\ 7 & {7}^{2} & {7}^{3} \\ 9 & {9}^{2} & {9}^{3}\end{aligned}]}}\overset{\beta }{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}{\beta }_{1} \\ {\beta }_{2} \\ {\beta }_{3}\end{aligned}]}} & =\overset{y}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 0 \\ -1 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $X$ is the design matrix, $\beta $ is the parameter vector, and $y$ is the observation vector.

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding an Expression for a Least-Squares Regression Curve
canonical_examples.problem:
| $x$ | **$0$** | **$1$** | **$2$** | **$3$** | **$4$** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $y$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ | $5$ | $2$ |

Consider the data above and the matrices below. Find an expression (in terms of $X$ and $\mathbf{y}$) for the vector of coefficients $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ of the curve $y=\beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \beta_2 x^2 + \beta_3 x^3$ that best fits the data. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14072333/assets/0329ad2c30d00d6051e2be094d076960d3ecfc35f9054feac195787f3af7328d.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The coefficients of the curve 

$$
y=\beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \beta_2 x^2 + \beta_3 x^3
$$

that best fits the data can be found as the least-squares solution ${\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}$ to the system 

$$
X \boldsymbol{\beta} = \mathbf{y},
$$

where $X$ is the design matrix, $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ is the parameter vector, and $\mathbf{y}$ is the observation vector.

Pre-multiplying this equation by $X^T,$ we obtain the corresponding normal equation

$$
X^T \! X {\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}} = X^T \mathbf{y}.
$$

Since the columns of $X$ are linearly independent, the matrix ${X^T}X$ is invertible and 

$$
{\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}} = (X^T \! X )^{-1} X^T \mathbf{y}.
$$
